Unified Data-Tech Solutions Ltd (Udtechs)

What the company does, in plain terms:
Udtechs is a system integrator. When a large business needs a data centre, cloud setup, networking or cybersecurity, a system integrator brings all the pieces together and makes them work as one. Think of it as the company that builds and connects the "engine rooms" of the digital world for other businesses.

The numbers, decoded:

Revenue for Q1 FY27 came in at around ₹106.23 crore, up from around ₹85.59 crore in the same quarter last year. That is a year-on-year growth of around 24.11%. In simple words, the company earned around a quarter more this time than it did in the same quarter a year ago.

The executable order book stood at around ₹100 crore plus as of July-end. An order book is work already won but not yet delivered. It gives some visibility on revenue that is already in hand.

Six new enterprise customers were added and billed during the quarter, including names such as Sun Pharma, Parle Agro and Apsara Plastic.
Winning recognisable customers is a sign the business is being trusted
with real work.

Two new OEM partners were added, Barracuda and Lightstorm. This widens
the range of products the company can offer and sell.

Why a novice should care:
Growing revenue while adding marquee customers and expanding the partner network is a healthy combination. The order book offers some comfort that this is not just a one quarter story.

The honest other side:
An order book of around ₹100 crore plus is close to a single quarter of revenue, so it is decent but not a multi-year cushion on its own. A business update is management's own framing. It highlights revenue and customer wins, but does not show margins, profit or cash flow. One strong top line quarter does not confirm the full year picture. System integration can also be a project lumpy, lower margin business, so the quality of profit matters as much as the growth number.

Lloyds Engineering enters into drone manufacturing — and this one's worth reading carefully.

LEWL's subsidiary Lloyds Advance Defence Systems Limited (LADS) has signed a formal agreement with FlyFocus, Poland for licensed manufacturing and joint R&D of UAV products in India.

Three things to note:

1. LEWL now has a dedicated defence subsidiary. The agreement runs through LADS, not the parent — which means the company has quietly set up a separate legal entity specifically for defence. That's a structure play, not just a partnership announcement.

2. This is a step up from the earlier MoU. The Oct-25 tie-up was intent. Today's filing is a licensed manufacturing + joint product development arrangement — actual commercial teeth.

3. Clean deal, no equity or RPT complications. No shares issued, no related-party angle, no promoter connection to FlyFocus. Straightforward arm's length agreement.

The bigger picture — LEWL is clearly positioning LADS as its dedicated defence vehicle, with FlyFocus as the technology anchor for the UAV segment. Watch this entity for further tie-ups as India's defence indigenisation orders start flowing.

~AUM grew by 62% YoY and 10% QoQ to 40,000 cr. 48% of the book is in gold loans. 17% of the book is in MSME segment, 20% of the book is in Housing Finance, and remaining in Construction Finance and other segments.

~NIMs expanded by 80 bps YoY to 9.7%, driven by both an increase in yield and a fall in cost of borrowing.

~The highest yielding segment is the gold loan segment, and the lowest yielding segment is the Housing Finance segment.

~PAT grew by over 100% in this quarter. RoAA(4%) and RoAE(19%) is also trending upwards.

~The growth in RoAA and RoAE is driven by margin expansion, higher fee income, and reduction in credit costs.

~Company’s target is to deliver consistent RoAE of 19.0% - 21.0% and RoAA of 4.2% - 4.7%

~The company has also started insurance distribution which is an asset light income stream. They are as of now focusing on selling insurance to existing customers, which is also known as cross-selling.

~Cost to income ratio also fell by 500 bps YoY to 44%.

~Cost to income ratio is expected to be around 47-50% in the medium term, and co-lending is targeted at 20% of the overall AUM.

reports.text:
India Built a Phone Export Industry. Now It Needs Customers It Doesn't Have.

India's handset export scheme is aimed at a global market where roughly 61% of units sit outside Apple and Samsung and are served by Chinese brands using Chinese assemblers. The binding constraint is therefore anchor customer access, not incentive quantum or installed capacity, which is why the same policy tool that worked domestically may not repeat offshore. 

This is falsified if a non Apple Indian assembler announces a multi year export contract with a top ten global brand.
